extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers and research funders interested in peer review and scholarly-publishing models
extracted.subtask_description: A broad survey of peer-review models, practices and proposed reforms used in scientific publishing, and the criteria each model uses to evaluate manuscripts or reviewers. Useful for stakeholders considering changes to peer-review policy or practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blind peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional model in which reviewers can see who the authors are, but the authors cannot see who the reviewers are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely used historically; criticized for bias (institution, race, country, personal biases). Reviewers' identities remain hidden from authors and readers and reports are seen only by editor(s) and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review in which authors' identities are concealed from reviewers (and often from editors), intended to reduce bias related to author identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey evidence shows many researchers prefer double-blind as more objective. Trials (Springer Nature, IOP) found authors opt into it in modest numbers and that double-blind submissions had different editorial outcomes (lower rates of being sent for external review and lower acceptance after review). Challenges include: preprints can reveal authorship; optional double-blind may itself create bias (referees/editors reacting to the choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple-blind peer review (editor blinding)
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension where professional editors make initial decisions without knowing the authors' identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed to address potential editor bias during initial triage; one possible response to observed differences in outcomes for double-blind submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open / transparent peer review (umbrella)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of models where some combination of reviewer identities, reviewer reports, or review processes are made public or transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a single definition—Ross-Hellauer identified 22 distinct forms; elements can be optional. Purported benefits include accountability, credit for reviewers, and training for early-career researchers; drawbacks include difficulty recruiting reviewers and potential chilling of critical reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing the names of the referees with the paper (one common trait of open peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages accountability and credit but can reduce willingness to review and may make junior reviewers less critical due to fear of retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports (publishing referee reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the content of referee reports publicly available alongside the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: BMJ publishes signed reports and prepublication history; some journals publish reports but keep reviewers anonymous. Publishing reports can provide transparency about the decision process and train others; reports can be given DOIs and credited to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open participation (crowd-sourced / public peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing broader community commenting and reviewing (any researcher in the field may review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can uncover diverse viewpoints and increase scrutiny, but requires infrastructure and moderation; used in some open models and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open pre-review manuscripts (preprints / public manuscripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making manuscripts available publicly before or during peer review (preprints or journal-hosted pre-review manuscripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increases visibility and can lead to identification of authors (complicating blinding); facilitates open discussion and rapid dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open interaction (consultative review / editor–referee discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitating interaction among editors and referees to agree on points authors must address (e.g., eLife's consultative model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision letters listing agreed points are published with accepted papers; individual reports may or may not be published. Encourages consensus and clarity in revision requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing decision letters and prepublication histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing editor decision letters, referee reports, author responses and earlier versions alongside the final article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ and EMBO Journal publish extensive prepublication histories; this approach promotes transparency about revisions and editorial reasoning. Not all journals require referees to sign reports in these models.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLOS ONE criterion: technical soundness over importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers judge whether a paper is technically sound and worthy of inclusion in the published scientific record, not whether it is important or significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model (typical for some mega-journals) separates soundness from perceived impact, reducing subjective judgments about novelty/importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive public peer review (discussion paper model)
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial editorial check for scope and technical standards followed by public posting as a 'discussion paper' for open commenting and designated referees; authors respond during an open discussion phase before revision and final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics; discussion phase typically lasts ~8 weeks; previous versions, comments and author responses remain available. Reported to deter low-quality submissions and can lead to low rejection rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: F1000Research model (post-publication author-led invited open peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles are published after basic checks (e.g., supporting data available) then undergo post-publication peer review by referees suggested by authors but vetted by editors; referee reports are published and can be assigned DOIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest referees; editors check suggestions (criteria: not close collaborators, appropriate expertise, no competing interests) and remain the contact point. Articles carry status labels (awaiting peer review, approved, approved with reservations, not approved). Acceptance for indexing requires specified combinations of approved ratings (e.g., two 'approved' or one 'approved' + two 'approved with reservations'). Infrastructure and editorial systems must support versioning and report association.

rubrics_metrics.name: F1000 / platform referee selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees suggested by authors are checked to ensure they are not close collaborators, have appropriate expertise, and have no competing interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial team formally invites reviewers only if they fit these criteria; preserves peer-review standards while using author-suggested reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic checks before publication (data/supporting materials availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial checks to ensure manuscripts meet minimum technical requirements before posting (for platforms like F1000Research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks include availability of supporting data and that the submission meets scope/technical thresholds; these are not full peer review but gate the platform for posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered reports (two-stage review focusing on methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 1: submission of hypotheses and detailed methods for peer review; if approved, the journal accepts the study in principle before data collection. Stage 2: after study completion, submission of results and discussion; final acceptance depends on adherence to the approved plan and whether conclusions are justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees at stage 1 evaluate hypotheses, experimental design, power, controls, and analysis plans. Data collection must not start until stage 1 acceptance. Allows exploratory analyses if clearly labelled. Intended to reduce publication bias and outcome switching; increasingly adopted across fields and used for clinical trials by some journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results-free peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors submit a partial manuscript containing rationale and methods but no results or discussion; if methods/rationale are acceptable, the paper is accepted in principle and later revised with results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accept-in-principle decision can only be revoked at stage 2 if results/discussion deviate unjustifiably from the stage 1 aims and methods. Used by BMC Psychology as an option to combat publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining funding and publication decisions (registered reports funding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pilot aligning grant funding decisions with journal publication in a two-stage process: researchers opt in during grant application, then submit a registered report for the funded work that uses the same referees where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to reduce reviewer burden and questionable research practices; success metrics include uptake, reviewer agreement, and downstream effects on research quality and publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recruitment and acceptance-rate effects by review model
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed differences in reviewers' willingness to accept review invitations depending on peer-review model (double-blind, single-blind, open).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited show higher accept rates for double-blind (e.g., 60%) and lower for open review (e.g., 42%), with single-blind intermediate (e.g., 53%). Open review reduces reviewer recruitment and may affect the pool and candor of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and attribution for reviewers (DOIs, ORCID)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning DOIs to referee reports and enabling inclusion in reviewers' ORCID profiles so reviewers receive formal credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some platforms (F1000Research) assign DOIs to reports; many journals that publish reports do not. Formal crediting can incentivize reviewing and make reviewer effort visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and professional arguments for openness (accountability, training, credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review is argued to increase accountability of editors and referees, provide credit for reviewers, and help train early-career researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents argue openness penalizes inadequate reviews and helps professional development; opponents cite potential retribution fears and reduced criticalness, especially for junior researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology and collaborative infrastructure to improve peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations to develop AI tools to find suitable referees, transfer reviews between publishers, detect inconsistencies automatically, and invest in reviewer training and collaboration among publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital Science/BMC report recommended: AI referee-finding, diversify reviewer pool, experiment with models, reviewer training programs, publisher cooperation, reviewer credit systems, and greater use of technology to detect issues difficult for humans to spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing publication bias, spin and outcome switching
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognising and mitigating practices that preferentially publish positive results or misreport trial outcomes; specific approaches include registered reports and results-free review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome switching (not reporting pre-specified outcomes or reporting unplanned ones) is a concern especially in clinical trials; registered reports and related models aim to prevent this and increase reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial triage by professional editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional editors make initial decisions on submissions (triage) and commonly desk-reject a large proportion before external peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nature journals' professional editors reject about 80% of submissions without external review. Triage decisions influence which manuscripts reach external review and can interact with blinding policies.
